Which of the drone companies do you work for, and what kind of drones do you look after?
transcript.answer: I don't know which specific drone operating company I work for, but we run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. These models differ in their carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, the sensors they carry, and the charging connectors they use. My job involves keeping these drones and our charging equipment in working order.

transcript.question: How do you find out which drones or charging equipment need your attention?

What tasks are involved in keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order?
transcript.answer: My work involves adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are fixed, and send them to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

transcript.answer: I don't know about a specific worst day. However, it worries me that radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

transcript.question: Can you give me a concrete example of a problem caused when drone reports arrive late, out of order, or not at all?

transcript.answer: I set up charging pads at our sites, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable. Each of our sites has a few dozen charging pads, and we never lend pads to another company.

transcript.question: Is there anything else about your responsibilities, the equipment, or the rules you follow that we haven't covered yet?
transcript.answer: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. transcript.question: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from start to finish?
transcript.answer: I plan and run flights for my drone operating company, deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off on flights before they leave. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight if needed. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control like whether a load is ready, how the drone reaches its job points, and when it arrives.

transcript.question: Tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months—what happened, and what made it so bad?
transcript.answer: Radio coverage was patchy in bad weather and around industrial sites, meaning reports from drones arrived late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Drones sometimes restarted in flight after a software fault and carried on, while closures were amended during the day and could even come into force while drones from several companies were already in the air. Batteries also drained faster in cold and wind than planned, and the server was updated and restarted during working hours while drones were flying, occasionally crashing.

transcript.question: When something goes wrong like that—whether a flight problem or a server crash—what is the very first thing you need to know right afterward?

transcript.question: Before you sign off on a flight to leave, what information do you look at to decide which drone to use and which way it should go?
transcript.answer: I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, but software never chooses a drone or a way for us.

transcript.question: What makes a drone suitable or able to get to where a job starts?
transcript.answer: Drones differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry like cameras, thermal cameras, or laser scanners, and which charging connector they use. Each drone has a home site, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company.

transcript.question: What kinds of jobs are you planning flights for, and how do their routes or job points differ?
transcript.answer: I plan deliveries that carry a load from one site to another, and inspections that take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order before bringing it back to the starting point. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have a limited number of places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

transcript.question: What determines when you need to call off a flight, either before it leaves or while it is in the air?
transcript.answer: I can call off a flight, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. Beyond that, I don't know.
